instructions: Fix only the findings listed below.
Never delete or change a must-keep item.
Split long sentences instead of cutting words.
Keep every condition, negation, number, name and code span.
Do not touch code blocks, paths, UI labels or quoted error text.
Leave paragraphs without findings as they are.
Save the result over the original file. Do not rename it.

rules.name: Time of day with AM or PM
rules.says: The guide writes times as a numeral, a space, and AM or PM in capitals. Noon and midnight are written as words.

rules.name: Opener that announces
rules.says: This opener says nothing the reader came for.

rules.name: Never "Are you sure?" or "Warning!" as a title
rules.says: A confirmation names the object and the consequence so the reader knows what they're deciding.

rules.name: Terms that carry bias
rules.says: The guide replaces this term. A term that's part of a command, a setting, or an API stays as written, so flag that case for the product team instead of editing the prose.

rules.name: Never leave a table cell blank
rules.says: A blank cell could mean none, not applicable, or forgotten.

rules.name: Use the owner's exact casing for brand names
rules.says: The brand table in the guide gives the owner's casing. Only the brands the guide itself prints are checked. Add your own rows to this rule when you fill in the brand table.

rules.name: Moreover, Furthermore, Additionally
rules.says: These connectors stitch paragraphs together without adding a fact. Each paragraph should stand on its own first sentence.

rules.name: Never "click here" as link text
rules.says: "Here" tells the reader nothing about where the link goes, and screen readers list links by their text.

rules.name: Combat and violence metaphors
rules.says: Combat language makes an ordinary action sound violent and translates badly. A technical term such as the `kill` command stays as written.

rules.name: Describe only what ships today
rules.says: A feature guide that describes a planned feature becomes a promise. The guide moves such statements to release notes or a roadmap. This is a flag for the author, not an edit.

rules.name: Condition after the instruction
rules.says: The condition comes after the instruction. A reader can do the step before reading that it does not apply.

rules.name: Straight quotation marks
rules.says: Curly quotation marks and apostrophes usually come from a word processor. They don't render the same everywhere, and they break copied values.

rules.name: Disability terms and metaphors
rules.says: Focus on people, not conditions, and don't borrow a disability as a metaphor.

rules.name: No em dashes
rules.says: The em dash is the strongest machine-written tell, and every job it does has a clearer replacement. A double hyphen is treated as an em dash in Markdown.

rules.name: Email, not e-mail
rules.says: The guide spells it as one word with no hyphen.

rules.name: No exclamation points
rules.says: An exclamation point reads as shouting in an error and as gushing in a success message.

rules.name: Filler intensifiers
rules.says: These words add emphasis but no fact. Inside a quotation or a product name they stay.

rules.name: Use present tense
rules.says: Product behavior that happens every time is described in the present tense. A real statement about timing ("will be available in the next release") is a fact and stays.

rules.name: Gender-neutral words
rules.says: The guide's table gives a gender-neutral word for this one.

rules.name: Gendered pronoun for a generic person
rules.says: A generic person, such as "the admin" or "a reviewer", gets no gendered pronoun. Gendered pronouns are right only for a named person who uses them and in direct quotations.

rules.name: No ampersands or plus signs in headings
rules.says: Symbols in a heading read as abbreviations and don't translate.

rules.name: No period or ellipsis at the end of a heading
rules.says: Headings and labels take no end punctuation other than a question mark.

rules.name: Headings use sentence case
rules.says: This heading looks like title case: two or more words after the first are capitalized. Proper nouns and acronyms stay capitalized, so check that the capitals are names.

rules.name: Alt text doesn't start with "Image of"
rules.says: A screen reader already announces that this is an image.

rules.name: Avoid Latin abbreviations
rules.says: Readers and translation tools misread Latin abbreviations.

rules.name: No semicolons, commas, or conjunctions at the ends of list items
rules.says: A list item stands on its own. Trailing punctuation or conjunctions turn the list back into a sentence.

rules.name: Start each list item with a capital letter
rules.says: List items start with a capital letter, even when they're fragments. A code value or identifier that must stay lowercase is the exception, and it belongs in code style.

rules.name: Marketing words that carry no fact
rules.says: This word makes a claim without a fact behind it. Say what the product does instead.

rules.name: No contractions in strict-plain
rules.says: Strict-plain text uses full forms. A contraction is easy to misread for readers of English as a second language, and the negative in 'can't' or 'don't' is easy to miss.

rules.name: Spell out zero through nine in prose
rules.says: In prose, counts below 10 are words. Numerals stay for measurements, durations, times, versions, percentages, identifiers, and when a sentence mixes numbers of the same kind above and below 10.

rules.name: Spell out the month in dates
rules.says: A numeric date reads differently in different countries. ISO dates belong in data formats, logs, and code.

rules.name: Don't write (s) for one or more
rules.says: "(s)" asks the reader to parse two sentences at once and breaks screen readers.

rules.name: No ordinals in dates
rules.says: The ordinal suffix adds nothing to a date.

rules.name: Passive voice
rules.says: A "was done by" sentence hides the actor at the end. The guide converts to active only when the actor is named or obvious, and keeps passive when it keeps blame off the reader or when the receiver is the point. Only passives with an explicit "by" are flagged.

rules.name: Percent in prose, % in UI and tables
rules.says: In running text the guide spells out "percent". The symbol is for UI strings and tables.

rules.name: Choose plain words
rules.says: The guide prefers the short, common word. "Enable" stays when it means turn on.

rules.name: No please, sorry, oops, or unfortunately
rules.says: Politeness words add length and, in an error, sound like blame or panic. Say what happened and what to do.

rules.name: Don't point with above or below
rules.says: Position breaks when the layout changes or a screen reader reads the page in order.

rules.name: Products don't think
rules.says: This gives the product a mind. The guide treats it as a claim for the author to confirm, not a style edit.

rules.name: Don't promise outcomes
rules.says: An unqualified promise is one the product can't keep, because results depend on the customer's data and configuration. This is a claim for the author, not a style edit.

rules.name: Name a month or quarter, not a season
rules.says: A season names different months in each hemisphere.

rules.name: Select, not click or tap
rules.says: "Select" works for every input method. Keys are still pressed.

rules.name: No semicolons
rules.says: A sentence that needs a semicolon is usually two sentences or a list.

rules.name: Sign in, not log in
rules.says: House style uses "sign in" as the verb and "sign-in" as the noun. A swap that would rename an existing UI label everywhere is a product decision, so flag that case rather than changing one screen.

rules.name: Don't use a slash for or
rules.says: A slash asks the reader to guess whether you mean "and", "or", or both. Fixed pairs such as on/off and read/write are fine.

rules.name: "Something went wrong" is the last resort
rules.says: A generic error gives the reader nothing to act on. If the cause is known, name it and say what to do.

rules.name: Steps are full sentences with a period
rules.says: Each step in a numbered procedure is a full sentence and ends with a period.

rules.name: Write to you, not the user
rules.says: The guide addresses the reader directly as "you". "The user" puts a third person between the product and the reader.

rules.name: Space between a number and its unit
rules.says: The unit is a separate word, and the percent sign is not.

rules.name: Don't use we to give advice
rules.says: Advice phrased as a wish or as the company's opinion is longer and softer than a command. The guide reserves "we" for times when the company must be the speaker, such as a privacy notice or an outage update.

rules.name: Cut words, not facts
rules.says: This phrase means the same as a shorter one. Every word should do work.

paragraphs.text: Acme Tasks keeps your team's projects, tasks, and deadlines in one place.
In today's fast-paced digital world, teams need one list they can trust.
Create a project in order to group related tasks.
The user can invite teammates from the project page.
Log in with your work email address.
We recommend that you turn on multifactor authentication.
Enter your e-mail address on the sign-in page.
Utilize filters to narrow the task list.
The board is very easy to scan.
Acme Tasks offers a powerful timeline view.
Export reports in common formats, e.g. CSV and PDF.
Each task has a title, a due date — and an owner.
Tasks sync every hour; comments sync right away.
Type “Today” to set the due date.
Select a project/task to open it.
The weekly report is generated by the scheduler.
When you select **Archive**, the project will move to the archive.
Two-way calendar sync is on the roadmap.
The assistant understands what you need.
Smart sorting guarantees that nothing slips.
Each attachment can be up to 25MB.
A new dashboard ships next spring.
Add trusted domains to the whitelist.
Each reviewer sees his own queue.
The help desk is manned around the clock.
A slow network can cripple the sync.
Are you sure you want to delete this project?
To view the sharing rules, click here.
For details, see the steps described above.
You need the Owner role on the project.
Every new task needs these three things.
Each plan includes a different level of support.
Connect your Github account to link commits to tasks.

findings.message: This opener says nothing the reader came for.
findings.fix: Delete it and start with the point.

findings.message: This heading looks like title case: two or more words after the first are capitalized. Proper nouns and acronyms stay capitalized, so check that the capitals are names.
findings.fix: Capitalize only the first word, proper nouns, and the first word after a colon.

findings.message: This phrase means the same as a shorter one. Every word should do work.
findings.fix: Use the short form from the guide's table.

findings.message: The guide addresses the reader directly as "you". "The user" puts a third person between the product and the reader.
findings.fix: Rewrite to "you" ("You get an email when someone assigns you a task"). Use "user" only as a category word, such as "user permissions", or in developer documentation where it means the end user of the reader's software.

findings.message: "Select" works for every input method. Keys are still pressed.
findings.fix: Use "select" for options, values, links, menu items, and buttons.

findings.message: The condition comes after the instruction. A reader can do the step before reading that it does not apply.
findings.fix: Move the condition to the front: 'If the sync stops, restart the service.'

findings.message: House style uses "sign in" as the verb and "sign-in" as the noun. A swap that would rename an existing UI label everywhere is a product decision, so flag that case rather than changing one screen.
findings.fix: Use "sign in" for the action and "sign-in" for the noun or adjective.

findings.message: Advice phrased as a wish or as the company's opinion is longer and softer than a command. The guide reserves "we" for times when the company must be the speaker, such as a privacy notice or an outage update.
findings.fix: Give the instruction as a command: "Back up the database before you upgrade."

findings.message: The guide spells it as one word with no hyphen.
findings.fix: Write "email".

findings.message: The guide prefers the short, common word. "Enable" stays when it means turn on.
findings.fix: Replace with the plain word. For "via", choose "through", "by", or "using" to fit the sentence.

findings.message: These words add emphasis but no fact. Inside a quotation or a product name they stay.
findings.fix: Delete the word, unless the sentence then loses a fact.

findings.message: This word makes a claim without a fact behind it. Say what the product does instead.
findings.fix: Delete it, or replace it with a concrete statement of behavior.

findings.message: Readers and translation tools misread Latin abbreviations.
findings.fix: Write "for example", "that is", or name the items. For "etc.", prefer "such as" before the list, or say what is included.

findings.message: The em dash is the strongest machine-written tell, and every job it does has a clearer replacement. A double hyphen is treated as an em dash in Markdown.
findings.fix: For an aside, use a pair of commas or parentheses. To introduce a list, use a colon. To join two statements, use a period and two sentences.

findings.message: A sentence that needs a semicolon is usually two sentences or a list.
findings.fix: Split the sentence, or turn the series into a list.

findings.message: An exclamation point reads as shouting in an error and as gushing in a success message.
findings.fix: End the sentence with a period.

findings.message: Curly quotation marks and apostrophes usually come from a word processor. They don't render the same everywhere, and they break copied values.
findings.fix: Replace with the straight character: " or '.

findings.message: Curly quotation marks and apostrophes usually come from a word processor. They don't render the same everywhere, and they break copied values.
findings.fix: Replace with the straight character: " or '.

findings.message: A slash asks the reader to guess whether you mean "and", "or", or both. Fixed pairs such as on/off and read/write are fine.
findings.fix: Write "or" (or "and"). "And/or" almost always means "or".

findings.message: A "was done by" sentence hides the actor at the end. The guide converts to active only when the actor is named or obvious, and keeps passive when it keeps blame off the reader or when the receiver is the point. Only passives with an explicit "by" are flagged.
findings.fix: Put the actor first: "The scheduler generates the report every Monday."

findings.message: Product behavior that happens every time is described in the present tense. A real statement about timing ("will be available in the next release") is a fact and stays.
findings.fix: Use the present tense: "the dialog closes".

findings.message: A feature guide that describes a planned feature becomes a promise. The guide moves such statements to release notes or a roadmap. This is a flag for the author, not an edit.
findings.fix: Flag it: is this released? If not, move it to the release notes or the roadmap.

findings.message: This gives the product a mind. The guide treats it as a claim for the author to confirm, not a style edit.
findings.fix: Flag it for the author and suggest a verb such as ranks, selects, estimates, predicts, or recommends.

findings.message: An unqualified promise is one the product can't keep, because results depend on the customer's data and configuration. This is a claim for the author, not a style edit.
findings.fix: Flag it. Suggest a plain statement of what the product does, or a verb such as ranks, selects, estimates, predicts, or recommends.

findings.message: In prose, counts below 10 are words. Numerals stay for measurements, durations, times, versions, percentages, identifiers, and when a sentence mixes numbers of the same kind above and below 10.
findings.fix: Write the word: "five projects".

findings.message: A numeric date reads differently in different countries. ISO dates belong in data formats, logs, and code.
findings.fix: Write "June 12, 2026".

findings.message: The ordinal suffix adds nothing to a date.
findings.fix: Write "June 1".

findings.message: The unit is a separate word, and the percent sign is not.
findings.fix: Write "25 MB" and "30 ms". In running text, write a percentage as "87 percent".

findings.message: In running text the guide spells out "percent". The symbol is for UI strings and tables.
findings.fix: Write "50 percent".

findings.message: The guide writes times as a numeral, a space, and AM or PM in capitals. Noon and midnight are written as words.
findings.fix: Write "10:45 AM", "noon", or "midnight".

findings.message: A season names different months in each hemisphere.
findings.fix: Name the month or the quarter: "in March" or "in Q1 2027".

findings.message: The guide replaces this term. A term that's part of a command, a setting, or an API stays as written, so flag that case for the product team instead of editing the prose.
findings.fix: Use the replacement from the table.

findings.message: A generic person, such as "the admin" or "a reviewer", gets no gendered pronoun. Gendered pronouns are right only for a named person who uses them and in direct quotations.
findings.fix: In order of preference: rewrite to "you", rewrite to a plural, use "the" or "a", name the role, or use singular "they".

findings.message: The guide's table gives a gender-neutral word for this one.
findings.fix: Use the replacement from the table.

findings.message: Combat language makes an ordinary action sound violent and translates badly. A technical term such as the `kill` command stays as written.
findings.fix: Use the plain word from the guide's table.

findings.message: Focus on people, not conditions, and don't borrow a disability as a metaphor.
findings.fix: Use the plain replacement. "The outage crippled the service" becomes "The outage stopped the service."

findings.message: Politeness words add length and, in an error, sound like blame or panic. Say what happened and what to do.
findings.fix: Delete the word and lead with the action.

findings.message: Strict-plain text uses full forms. A contraction is easy to misread for readers of English as a second language, and the negative in 'can't' or 'don't' is easy to miss.
findings.fix: Write the full form, for example 'do not' or 'cannot'.

findings.message: A confirmation names the object and the consequence so the reader knows what they're deciding.
findings.fix: Name the action and the object: "Delete this project? Its tasks move to your default project."

findings.message: A generic error gives the reader nothing to act on. If the cause is known, name it and say what to do.
findings.fix: Write one message per known cause: what happened, why if the reader can act on it, and what to do next.

findings.message: "Here" tells the reader nothing about where the link goes, and screen readers list links by their text.
findings.fix: Name the destination or the result: "View the sharing rules."

findings.message: Position breaks when the layout changes or a screen reader reads the page in order.
findings.fix: Name the section and link to it, or name the control.

findings.message: A screen reader already announces that this is an image.
findings.fix: Describe what the image shows or does: "The Sharing tab with Invite people selected."

findings.message: Each step in a numbered procedure is a full sentence and ends with a period.
findings.fix: Add the period.

findings.message: List items start with a capital letter, even when they're fragments. A code value or identifier that must stay lowercase is the exception, and it belongs in code style.
findings.fix: Capitalize the first word, or put a lowercase identifier in code style.

findings.message: A list item stands on its own. Trailing punctuation or conjunctions turn the list back into a sentence.
findings.fix: Remove the trailing semicolon, comma, or conjunction.

findings.message: A blank cell could mean none, not applicable, or forgotten.
findings.fix: Write "None" or "Not applicable". If you don't know which, flag it.

findings.message: Symbols in a heading read as abbreviations and don't translate.
findings.fix: Write "and".

findings.message: These connectors stitch paragraphs together without adding a fact. Each paragraph should stand on its own first sentence.
findings.fix: Delete the connector. If the paragraphs need a link, make it a fact.

findings.message: The brand table in the guide gives the owner's casing. Only the brands the guide itself prints are checked. Add your own rows to this rule when you fill in the brand table.
findings.fix: Use the casing from the brand table.

findings.message: "(s)" asks the reader to parse two sentences at once and breaks screen readers.
findings.fix: Write "one or more files", or use the plural.

findings.message: Headings and labels take no end punctuation other than a question mark.
findings.fix: Remove the period or ellipsis.
